messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Frank had been working late at the hotel he managed when the mugging happened, leaving through the service entrance after a long evening of checking staffing and closing paperwork. It was dark, the lobby noise had thinned, and he was walking to his car with his keys in hand when two men approached from the side of the building. One moved too quickly for Frank to read his intentions, and what stayed with him afterward was the sense that they looked suspicious before anything was even said. He could smell alcohol on them before he understood the danger, a harsh, sour odor that seemed to announce recklessness and trouble. When one of the men barked at him and the other stepped in close, Frank was struck by the suddenness of it, by the feeling that the situation had shifted in an instant from ordinary to unsafe. The episode ended with him being robbed, but he remembered the humiliation of it most vividly: standing there as if reduced in front of strangers, unable to stop what was happening and painfully aware of how exposed he had been.

In the weeks that followed, Frank found himself returning to that moment in fragments. At work, any man lingering near the entrance, any guest who seemed watchful in the wrong way or moved with a little too much purpose, could make him tense before he had time to think. He was especially unsettled if someone appeared suspiciously near the service corridor or hovered by the parking area after dark. Even if nothing happened, he would keep watching, scanning faces and hands, checking who was coming and going, and mentally rehearsing where he could stand if trouble started. Loud noises were another immediate jolt for him. A door slamming in the kitchen, a dropped tray, a car backfiring in the lot, or the sharp bang of a suitcase hitting tile could send a spike of alarm through him before he had sorted out what caused it. He described it as his body reacting first, his mind catching up later.

At home, Frank had not been able to leave the fear behind at the hotel. He reported feeling on guard even inside his own house, as if being indoors no longer fully separated him from danger. If a car pulled up too fast outside, if voices rose on the street, or if he heard a sudden crash from another room, he was instantly alert. His wife learned not to come up behind him without warning, because when she touched his shoulder unexpectedly he reacted with visible alarm, jerking away and turning sharply as though preparing for an attack. He hated that response and felt embarrassed by it, but it happened quickly enough that he could not always stop it.

Over time, Frank came to believe that people could not be trusted. That belief sat beneath much of what he did now. At the hotel, where his job required him to greet strangers, solve problems, and keep the place running smoothly, he had become more guarded with guests and staff alike. He did not think everyone meant harm, but he felt that assumptions of goodwill were naïve, and he watched for signs that someone might be unstable, intoxicated, or planning something. The smell of alcohol in particular still tightened his chest and brought back the memory of the men approaching him that night. He noticed it in the lobby bar, on guests passing by, even in the hallway when a resident had been drinking. Each time, he felt the old warning rise in him, and he would become more watchful without announcing why.

Frank also spoke with painful consistency about feeling permanently humiliated by what had happened. It was not only that he had been robbed; it was that, in his own mind, the event had marked him as someone who could be cornered and made helpless. He said that he had spent most of his life being capable and composed, the sort of man colleagues relied on, and the mugging had left him feeling stripped of that image. He continued to work, but he found himself less comfortable in the hotel’s public spaces and more eager to be behind the desk or in a back office where he could see the entrances. The world, to him, no longer felt ordinary or broadly safe. He had come to see it as a dangerous place where harm could arrive quickly and without warning, from people who looked normal until they did not.

By the time he sought help, Frank was tired of living this way. He was not seeking reassurance that the robbery had been “in the past”; what brought him in was the sense that he could not turn off the alertness, even in his own home or in the workplace he had once moved through with ease. He wanted to feel less on edge, less startled, and less ashamed of his own reactions. More than anything, he hoped to stop feeling as though danger might be waiting at every entrance, every loud sound, and every unfamiliar face.
